description: Simurg Takımı olarak, Türk mitolojisinin yeniden doğuşu, bilgeliği ve gücü simgeleyen efsanevi kuşundan ilham alıyoruz. NASA Space Apps Challenge’da bilim, teknoloji ve yaratıcılığı bir araya getirerek gerçek dünya problemlerine yenilikçi ve etkili çözümler geliştirmeyi hedefliyoruz.
summary:
A spacecraft can carry the right instruments and still fail to return useful science. Students rarely get to explore how design choices, flight plans, limited resources, and operational decisions interact across an entire mission.

Europa Clipper: Mission Lab brings those connections into a browser-based game inspired by NASA’s investigation of Europa. Players choose a scientific question, build a spacecraft, review its feasibility, and conduct three Europa flybys. They manage power, propellant, storage, and communication while responding to problems that their earlier choices help determine.

The mission continues after data collection. Players decide what to transmit to Earth, distinguish measurements from interpretations, and receive a report connecting their decisions to the outcome. Feedback and achievement badges encourage another attempt with a better-informed design.

NASA and JPL mission resources, Galileo findings, and Webb observations provide the scientific foundation. Available in English and Turkish, the game gives students and space enthusiasts an accessible way to practise systems thinking and evidence-based decision-making: choosing what a mission should investigate, what it can afford, and what its results actually support.
details:
A mission begins with a question. Every engineering choice should help answer it.

We built Europa Clipper: Mission Lab to let players experience the consequences of those choices across a complete mission. A larger instrument suite may offer more observations, but it also needs more power, storage, and launch capacity. A successful observation can still contribute little if the spacecraft cannot send its data home. These connections are the centre of the game.

FROM A SCIENCE QUESTION TO A SPACECRAFT

Players begin by choosing an investigation: Europa’s ice-shell structure, surface composition, or evidence for its subsurface ocean. This goal gives their design a purpose. Instrument descriptions explain what each measurement can contribute, helping beginners make informed choices.

Players configure their spacecraft, select a launcher and route, and balance instruments against supporting systems such as batteries, antennas, shielding, and propellant reserves. The interactive 3D spacecraft changes with the configuration. A design review checks the mission across its launch, space, ground, and user segments before the player proceeds.

Optional companion probes add another design trade-off: an additional viewpoint requires capacity and resources. These probes are explicitly presented as hypothetical game extensions.

OPERATING THE MISSION

An interactive launch and cruise sequence leads into three Europa flybys within a Jupiter-orbit mission scenario. Players choose research regions, observation plans, and active instruments while monitoring their resources.

Earlier decisions shape the problems they face and the solutions available. During an eclipse, for example, a power-hungry instrument selection can exceed the available battery energy. The player must decide whether to switch off an instrument or shorten observations. A choice made during spacecraft design now changes the science the mission can return.

Retargeting consumes propellant. Observations fill the recorder. Radiation-related events can disrupt instruments. Limited ground-station contact forces players to prioritise which datasets reach Earth. The game connects these decisions rather than treating each stage as an isolated exercise.

LEARNING FROM THE RESULT

The final report compares the original plan with the mission that actually unfolded. It brings together manoeuvres, propellant use, returned data, and unanswered scientific questions.

Players also classify scientific statements as measured, inferred, or unknown. Feedback explains what their evidence supports and where a stronger claim would need additional observations. Achievement badges recognise behaviours such as returning data, preserving propellant, and avoiding unsupported claims.

The report offers specific suggestions for another attempt. Players can change their configuration and explore whether a different design would have avoided a problem or supported their scientific goal more effectively.

WHY EUROPA AND NASA RESOURCES MATTER

Europa offers a compelling setting because evidence for a subsurface ocean connects planetary exploration with the question of potentially habitable environments beyond Earth. Galileo findings and Webb observations give players an existing scientific foundation, while Europa Clipper’s objectives and instruments connect their decisions to an active NASA mission.

NASA’s mission-design resources also shaped the game’s structure. The four mission segments inform the design review; JPL Concept Maturity Levels inspired the progression from a goal to a reviewed concept; and the Mission Design Lab informed the treatment of engineering trade-offs. An in-game Evidence Library makes the sources and their relevance accessible to players.

TECHNOLOGY AND MODELLING

The prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for interactive 3D graphics and the Web Audio API for synthesised sound. It is hosted on Netlify and supports English, Turkish, solo play, and shared-device role-based play for up to four participants.

The educational model tracks energy, data capacity, communication opportunities, and propellant use. Propellant estimates depend on spacecraft mass, assumed engine performance, and scenario-defined manoeuvres. Published NASA reference values, model assumptions, and abstract game units are identified separately. The displayed flight paths are illustrative rather than computed trajectory solutions.

INTENDED IMPACT

Our goal is to help students and space enthusiasts connect scientific ambition with engineering constraints. Clear explanations support first-time players, while competing priorities give more experienced players decisions to explore.

The next development priority is classroom testing with students and educators to assess usability, identify misconceptions, and evaluate learning outcomes. The current prototype provides a working foundation for that process.
